title: Ptosis Surgery in Poor Bell's Phenomenon: A Surgical Imperative
summary: Managing ptosis in patients with poor or absent Bell’s phenomenon is a high-stakes clinical challenge, requiring precise surgical planning to prevent exposure keratopathy. This guide outlines the evidence-based assessment and modified surgical strategies essential for safeguarding ocular surface integrity.

sections.title: Clinical Significance of Bell's Phenomenon
sections.content: Bell’s phenomenon is the reflexive superior and outward rotation of the globe upon eyelid closure. In patients with poor Bell's, the cornea remains exposed during sleep (lagophthalmos). Performing standard ptosis surgery (e.g., Fasanella-Servat or maximal levator advancement) in these patients can lead to severe exposure keratopathy, corneal ulceration, and vision loss.

sections.title: Risk Factors for Poor Bell's
content: Neurotrophic keratopathy
CN VII palsy (Facial nerve dysfunction)
Severe dry eye (Aqueous deficient)
History of chronic orbital/eyelid surgery
Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM)
Senile orbicularis weakness

sections.title: Red Flags: Pre-Surgical Assessment
content: Incomplete lid closure at rest
Positive Schirmer I test < 5mm
Corneal staining patterns in the inferior third
Decreased corneal sensitivity
Current history of filamentary keratitis

sections.title: Pre-operative Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Perform complete ocular surface exam including slit-lamp with fluorescein/lissamine green.
Step 2: Assess Bell's phenomenon: Ask patient to close eyes tightly while you manually elevate the upper lid.
Step 3: Measure Marginal Reflex Distance 1 (MRD1) and Levator Function (LF).
Step 4: Conduct Schirmer's I test (without anesthesia) and TBUT (Tear Break-Up Time).
Step 5: Perform the 'Phenylephrine Test' to simulate eyelid height and observe for induced lagophthalmos.

content.explanation: B: Break-up time (TBUT), E: Examination of cornea, L: Lubrication status, L: Levator function, S: Schirmer test.

sections.title: Post-Operative Management
content: Aggressive lubrication: Preservative-free artificial tears hourly
Nocturnal protection: Lacri-Lube or heavy ointment at night
Eyelid taping if persistent lagophthalmos is noted
Follow-up at Day 1, Week 1, Month 1, and Month 3
Immediate assessment if pain or photophobia occurs

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always under-correct in doubtful cases; it is easier to revise a ptosis than to treat a melting cornea.
A small lateral tarsorrhaphy can be combined with ptosis repair if the ocular surface is borderline.
Check corneal sensitivity: diminished sensitivity is a major risk factor for surgical complication.
The presence of a Bell’s phenomenon is a neuro-muscular integrity indicator; its absence suggests a higher risk of lagophthalmos.
